Here are the verse‑by‑verse notes on Psalm 23, drawn from the sources I was able to reach. I have noted where I could not obtain material for certain requested perspectives.

---

## Psalm 23 – Verse‑by‑Verse Notes

### Title and Overall Structure

The psalm bears the simple title “A Psalm of David.” David Guzik notes that most account it to be a psalm of David’s maturity, written with vivid remembrance of his youth as a shepherd (Spurgeon wrote, “I like to recall the fact that this psalm was written by David, probably when he was a king”). The psalm falls into two clear metaphors: vv. 1–4 picture the LORD as Shepherd; vv. 5–6 picture the LORD as a gracious Host at a banquet.

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-23/

Ellicott notes that “the mention of the house of Jehovah seems decisive against the Davidic authorship,” and suggests that if David’s fortunes coloured the psalm, it must have been “through the mind of some later writer.” He also notes that the Rabbis favoured allegorical readings — the return from exile or the guidance of Israel from Egypt through the wilderness — rather than reading it as a personal experience.

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/23.htm

---

### v. 1 — “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.”

**Traditional Reading (Gill, Guzik, Spurgeon, Pulpit):**

Gill (Baptist, 18th c.) identifies “the LORD” as Jehovah the Son, the Good Shepherd of John 10, to whom the shepherd office is most frequently ascribed in Scripture. David calls Him “*my* shepherd,” expressing personal faith, interest in Him, affection, and joy. From this he concludes “I shall not want” — not any temporal good thing the Shepherd sees fit, nor any spiritual good thing, since all fullness is in Christ. Gill also notes the Hebrew can be rendered “I shall not fail” or “come short” of eternal glory.

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/23.htm

David Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic, Enduring Word) explains that “I shall not want” functions both as a declaration (“all my needs are supplied by the LORD”) *and* as a decision (“I decide to not desire more than what the LORD gives”). He emphasises that the shepherd metaphor was especially intimate for David, who had been a literal shepherd. Kidner is quoted: “the shepherd lives with his flock and is everything to it: guide, physician and protector.”

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-23/

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the shepherd metaphor appears first plainly in the Davidic psalms and was “specially consecrated to us by our Lord’s employment and endorsement of it (John 10:11-16).” The Prayer‑Book Version renders the second half, “Therefore can I lack nothing.”

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/23.htm (search excerpt)

Barnes’ Notes: “I shall not want” is the *main idea* of the psalm, and it embraces everything that could be a proper object of desire — temporal or spiritual, body or soul, time or eternity. There is no reason to limit it to temporal necessities.

**Source:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-23.html (search excerpt)

Precept Austin collates multiple voices: Spurgeon says, “The wicked always want, but the righteous never”; the affirmation means the heart of a sheep is utterly satisfied with the Shepherd. The site also connects this to the OT names of God — e.g., Jehovah‑Jireh (“the LORD will provide”), Jehovah‑Raah (“the LORD my shepherd”).

**Source:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-23-commentary

**Reformed view (Ligonier):** “Psalm 23 opens with a revelation of God’s abundant provision for His people. Verses 1–3 emphasise the comprehensiveness of our Father’s care, encompassing both physical and spiritual needs.” John Calvin is quoted: “all men, it is true, are not treated with the same generosity with which David was treated; but there is not an individual who is not under obligation to God by the benefits which God has conferred upon him.”

**Source:** https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-our-shepherd (search excerpt)

**Other views — modern scholarship:** The NET Bible notes (cited at Precept Austin) observe that in vv. 1–4 “the psalmist pictures the Lord as a shepherd who provides for his needs and protects him from danger. The psalmist declares, ‘The Lord is my shepherd,’ and then extends and develops that metaphor, speaking as if he were a sheep.”

**Source:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-23-commentary

---

### v. 2 — “He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters.”

**Traditional Reading:**

Gill interprets the “green pastures” (Hebrew: “pastures of tender grass”) as the covenant of grace, the fullness of grace in Christ, the doctrines and ordinances of the Gospel. To “lie down” denotes satiety, fullness, rest, and safety. The “still waters” (or “waters of rest and quietness”) are the everlasting love of God, communion with God, Christ Himself as the fountain of living waters, the graces of the Spirit, and the Scriptures.

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/23.htm

David Guzik notes that the image is of the shepherd *making* the sheep lie down — a sheep does not always know what it needs and requires the shepherd’s help. He references Philip Keller’s insight (*A Shepherd Looks at Psalm 23*) that sheep will not lie down unless the shepherd has dealt with four things: fear, friction among the sheep, flies/parasites, and famine. Rest comes because the shepherd has addressed all four.

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-23/

Ellicott writes that the verbs are presents, not futures, describing the poet’s customary condition: “The psalmist describes himself as one of Jehovah’s flock, safe under His care, absolved from all anxieties … gaining from this confidence of safety the leisure to enjoy, without satiety, all the simple pleasures which make up life — the freshness of the meadow, the coolness of the stream.” He calls it “the most complete picture of happiness that ever was or can be drawn.”

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/23.htm

The Pulpit Commentary: “He maketh me to lie down in green pastures; literally, in grassy homesteads — ‘the richer, oasis‑like spots, where a homestead would be fixed in a barren tract of land’ (Kay).” “Still waters” is rendered “waters of refreshment” (LXX: ἐπὶ ὕδατος ἀναπαύσεως).

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/23.htm

Precept Austin summarises the line as “That’s Rest!” and “That’s Refreshment!” — part of its popular outline of the psalm.

**Source:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-23-commentary

---

### v. 3 — “He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name.”

**Traditional Reading:**

Gill explains “He restoreth my soul” in two ways: (a) when the sheep backslides or is driven away, the Shepherd brings it back and heals its backslidings; (b) when the soul is fainting and ready to die away, He revives, refreshes, and comforts it with discoveries of His love, the promises of His word, and the consolations of the Spirit. “He leadeth me in the paths of righteousness” refers to the plain paths of truth and holiness, and also to walking by faith in Christ and His righteousness. All this He does “for His name’s sake” — for His own glory, not for any merit in men.

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/23.htm

Guzik notes that “restores” has the idea of the rescue of a lost one — “it may picture the straying sheep brought back” (Kidner). Boice adds: “In Hebrew the words ‘restores my soul’ can mean ‘brings me to repentance’ (or conversion).” The shepherd’s guidance has a moral aspect — He leads into righteousness, for the credit and glory of His own name.

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-23/

Ellicott simply glosses “restoreth my soul” as “refresheth, recreateth, quickeneth,” and “for His name’s sake” means God’s providential dealings are in accord with His character for great graciousness.

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/23.htm

Pulpit Commentary: “He restoreth my soul; i.e., revives it and reinvigorates it when it is exhausted and weary.” The “paths of righteousness” are also “paths of pleasantness and peace” (Prov. 3:17).

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/23.htm

Precept Austin tags this verse as “That’s Healing!” and “That’s Guidance!” and “That’s Purpose!”

**Source:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-23-commentary

---

### v. 4 — “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.”

**Traditional Reading:**

Gill: “the valley of the shadow of death” does not refer primarily to spiritual darkness or desertion (since the psalmist says the Lord *is* with him), but to severe affliction, dark providences, or the approach of death itself. He notes the Targum interprets it of captivity; Jarchi and Kimchi of the wilderness of Ziph where David was pursued. “I will fear no evil” — neither Satan, nor evil men, nor any calamity, because everything is determined by God and works for good. The “rod” and “staff” Gill interprets as the Word of God (the rod of Christ’s strength) and the promises (the staff), which comfort the believer; also the shepherd’s crook by which the sheep are counted, guided, and protected from predators.

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/23.htm

Guzik emphasises the shift from “He” (vv. 1–3) to “You” (v. 4) — precisely at the moment of greatest danger, the Shepherd draws near. The “valley” suggests being hedged in; it is the *shadow* of death, not its substance (for the believer, Jesus took the full reality of death). Spurgeon is quoted: “Death in its substance has been removed, and only the shadow of it remains…. Nobody is afraid of a shadow.” Guzik also notes Kidner on the rod (a cudgel for defence, cf. 1 Sam. 17:35) and staff (for control and rounding up the flock — “discipline is security”). Maclaren thinks both names refer to one instrument used for beating off predators and directing sheep.

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-23/

Ellicott makes an important textual point: the Hebrew *tsal-māveth* (“shadow of death”) was probably on Hebrew lips “nothing more than a forcible synonym for a dark, gloomy place.” He suggests the reading should perhaps be *tsalmûth* (“shadow, darkness”). He lists its varied uses: the grave/underworld (Job 10:21–22), the darkness of a dungeon (Ps. 107:10), the pathless desert (Jer. 2:6), the blinding darkness of a sandstorm, and metaphorically of affliction (Isa. 9:2). “By valley we must understand a deep ravine. Palestine abounds in wild and gloomy valleys, and shepherd life experiences the actual peril of them.”

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/23.htm

Pulpit Commentary: “A sudden transition and contrast, such as David loved. The quiet paths of righteousness and peace remind the poet of the exact opposite — the dark and dismal way through the valley of the shadow of death.” It adds that the “valley” must not be limited to the actual approach of death; “it may stand for any crisis of danger, suffering, or weakness, bodily or spiritual.”

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/23.htm

**Reformed view (Ligonier):** “In the ancient world, shepherds carried a rod to club predators and drive them away, and a staff to guide their sheep, to keep them in line lest they go astray. Such guidance could be painful to the sheep at times as they were poked and prodded … Likewise, the discipline of the Lord can seem uncomfortable, but it is a comfort to us because, as Augustine writes, it shows that God is mindful of us.” The site also ties the “valley” to dangerous mountain paths in the Holy Land that shepherds had to traverse to find new watering holes.

**Source:** https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-our-shepherd (search excerpt) and https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-shepherding-god (search excerpt)

---

### v. 5 — “You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.”

**Traditional Reading:**

Gill interprets the “table” in three ways: (a) providential — a sufficiency of temporal good things; (b) in grace — the provisions of God’s house, the table of the Lord (His flesh and blood); (c) in glory — the joys of heaven compared to a feast. “In the presence of my enemies” — they look on and envy but cannot prevent the blessing. The “anointing with oil” points to the oil of gladness, the Spirit of God and His graces, filling the believer with spiritual joy — alluding to the Eastern custom of anointing guests’ heads at feasts. “My cup runneth over” denotes an affluence of both temporal and spiritual blessings.

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/23.htm

Guzik notes the metaphor shifts from Shepherd to Host without departing from the valley imagery. “The prepared table in the presence of enemies teaches us that God’s goodness and bounty don’t eliminate our conflicts but enable us to experience His care even in the midst of them.” Maclaren: “This is the condition of God’s servant — always conflict, but always a spread table.” Spurgeon: “Nothing is hurried, there is no confusion, no disturbance, the enemy is at the door and yet God prepares a table, and the Christian sits down and eats as if everything were in perfect peace.”

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-23/

Ellicott: “Such a sudden transition from the figure of the flock to that of a banquet is characteristic of Hebrew poetry.” “In the presence of mine enemies — We must imagine the banquet spread on some secure mountain height, in sight of the baffled foe, who look on in harmless spite.” “My cup runneth over” is literally “My cup is abundant drink.” The LXX reads, “Thine intoxicating cup, how excellent it is.”

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/23.htm

Pulpit Commentary: David reverts to the thought of tranquil, happy times. His adversaries are powerless; they have to “look on with ill‑concealed annoyance at his prosperity.” Ancient custom anointed honoured guests; the overflowing cup is “an expressive metaphor, indicative of a state of bliss rarely experienced in this life.”

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/23.htm

Precept Austin tags this as “That’s Hope!” (table in presence of enemies), “That’s Consecration!” (anointing), and “That’s Abundance!” (overflowing cup).

**Source:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-23-commentary

**Reformed view (Ligonier):** “Notably, Psalm 23 promises divine protection, not an easy life. God gives us a table in the midst of our enemies; He does not eradicate our foes all at once (v. 5). But He does work to give us rest and refreshment, even when these enemies are at the door.”

**Source:** https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-shepherding-god (search excerpt)

---

### v. 6 — “Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever.”

**Traditional Reading:**

Gill: “Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me” — either the free grace, love, favour, and mercy of God in Christ, or the effects of it (temporal and spiritual good things). The Hebrew can be rendered “only goodness and mercy” — nothing but mere mercy and kindness; though afflictions attend the child of God, these are in mercy and love, not wrath. “All the days of my life” — mercies are new every morning and continue until life ends. “I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever” may denote constant attendance on public worship (from which David had been deprived), or membership in the church as a pillar in God’s temple, or the assurance of dwelling in the heavenly house not made with hands. The Targum interprets it of the house of the sanctuary.

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/23.htm

Guzik: “Goodness and mercy” — Kidner notes “mercy” is the covenant‑word “steadfast love.” Meyer: “We are well escorted, with a Shepherd in front and these twin angels behind!” Spurgeon: “These twin guardian angels will always be with me at my back and my beck.” “I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever” — Kidner explains: “In the Old Testament world, to eat and drink at someone’s table created a bond of mutual loyalty, and could be the culminated token of a covenant…. So to be God’s guest is to be more than an acquaintance, invited for a day. It is to live with Him.” Spurgeon adds: “While I am here I will be a child at home with my God; the whole world shall be his house to me; and when I ascend into the upper chamber … I shall only go to dwell in the upper story of the house of the Lord for ever.”

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-23/

Ellicott makes a key translational point: “As the text stands it must be translated *I will return* (and abide) in the house of Jehovah.” He says “the house of the Lord can hardly be anything but the Temple; though some commentators treat this even as figurative of membership in the Divine family.”

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/23.htm

Pulpit Commentary: “The past is an earnest of the future.” It compares Psalm 27:4 (“One thing have I desired … that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life”) and says such passages “are, of course, not to be understood literally; they express the longing of the soul for a sense of the continual presence of God, and a realization of constant communion with him.”

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/23.htm

Precept Austin tags the final phrases as “That’s Blessing!” (goodness and mercy), “That’s Security!” (dwelling in God’s house), and “That’s Eternity!” (forever).

**Source:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-23-commentary

---

## Denominational Distinctives

Of the specific traditions requested, I was able to retrieve material from the following:

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasises God’s sovereignty in the psalm — the Shepherd’s “rod” and “staff” include the comfort of divine *discipline* (citing Augustine). The psalm promises protection *in* the presence of enemies, not the elimination of enemies — God’s people are not promised an easy life. David’s hope of feasting in God’s presence points to final vindication before all, including his enemies.

  **Source:** https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-our-shepherd and https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-shepherding-god (both via search excerpts)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** The reading closely follows the broad evangelical tradition while emphasising personal, experiential dimensions — e.g., the “He” to “You” shift as the Shepherd drawing near in crisis; Keller’s practical shepherding insights; the personal decision to “not want” more than God gives.

  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-23/

- **Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon via Guzik/Precept Austin):** Gill provides a thoroughly Christocentric reading — the Shepherd is specifically Jehovah the Son; the green pastures are the covenant of grace, Gospel ordinances, and the righteousness of Christ; the house of the Lord includes both the church on earth and the heavenly mansion. Spurgeon (widely quoted in the sources) stresses personal appropriation (“*My* shepherd”), the sufficiency of Christ for every need, and reads the whole psalm through the lens of the cross (Psalm 22 precedes Psalm 23).

  **Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/23.htm and quotations in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-23/ and https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-23-commentary

**What I could not retrieve (due to tool limits):** Dedicated verse‑by‑verse treatments from specifically Methodist/Wesleyan sites (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu), Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Anglican sources, Catholic sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox sites (oca.org), modern scholarly sites (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org in full), or prosperity/Word of Faith/hyper‑grace teachers could not be fetched in this session. The NET Bible notes summary appeared via Precept Austin (noted above), but the full notes page could not be accessed.

---

## Summary of Key Observations Across Traditions

1. **The “Shepherd to Host” shift:** All the traditional commentaries note that the psalm moves from the shepherd metaphor (vv. 1–4) to the host/banquet metaphor (vv. 5–6). The NET Bible note summarises this clearly: the psalmist is “a guest of honour and recipient of divine favour, who enjoys unlimited access to the divine palace.”

2. **“Valley of the shadow of death”:** Ellicott’s textual note is important — the Hebrew may simply mean “deep darkness” and is used for dungeons, deserts, sandstorms, and affliction, not exclusively for death. The traditional reading, however (made famous by Bunyan’s *Pilgrim’s Progress*), has always applied it pastorally to the believer’s passage through death and extreme trial.

3. **“I will dwell” or “I will return”:** Ellicott’s point that the Hebrew verb means “I will return (and abide)” adds a nuance — it may imply returning to the Temple repeatedly, not merely permanent residence. Both older and newer commentators see the phrase as ultimately pointing to eternal communion with God.

4. **The personal possessive:** Every source emphasises the importance of “*my* shepherd” — the psalm is a personal confession of trust, not merely a general statement about God.
